# Disability Language Style Guide
[**An Italian version of the guide is available here.**](https://group.intesasanpaolo.com/content/dam/portalgroup/repository-documenti/newsroom/news/Le_parole_giuste_media_e_persone_con_disabilit%C3%A0.pdf)

...

First, we would like to offer some basic guidelines:

...

## Able-bodied
### Mental illness/mental disorder
**Background:** “Mental illness” is an umbrella term for many different conditions that affect how individuals act, think, feel or perceive the world. The most common forms of mental illness are anxiety disorders, mood disorders and schizophrenia. Severity and symptoms vary widely.

...

### Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
**Background:** Post-traumatic stress disorder is an anxiety disorder usually caused by an extremely emotional traumatic event. Such events may include assault, war, sexual assault, natural disasters, car accidents or imprisonment.

...

### Suffers from/victim of/afflicted with/stricken with
**NCDJ Recommendation:** It is preferable to use neutral language when describing a person who has a disability, simply stating the facts about the nature of the disability. For example: “He has muscular dystrophy,” and avoiding characterizing those conditions as afflictions.

# Exploring Anxiety in Fiction: A Deep Dive into Characters with Anxiety Disorders
## The Spectrum of Anxiety Disorders Across Fictional Characters
### DSM-5 Anxiety Disorders vs. Fictional Representation Frequency
| Anxiety Disorder (DSM-5) | Estimated Real-World Prevalence (%) | Fictional Representation Frequency | Most Cited Fictional Example | Representation Gap |
| **Social Anxiety Disorder** | 7–12% | Medium | Neville Longbottom (*Harry Potter*) | Slightly under-represented |
| **Panic Disorder** | 1.5–3.5% | High | Tony Soprano (*The Sopranos*) | Over-represented |

...

## Do Fictional Portrayals of Anxiety Help Reduce Mental Health Stigma?
The caveat: not all portrayals qualify. Anxiety played for laughs, anxiety as a personality quirk, anxiety resolved by a single brave act, these don’t humanize.
They caricature. And caricature doesn’t reduce stigma. It redistributes it.

sources.title: A Disability Language Style Guide – Franklin County Public Health
sources.excerpt:
# A Disability Language Style Guide
## Consider helpful resources:
### 3. ******Avoid descriptions that imply pity****** .
Disability does not equal suffering! Terms like “afflicted with,” “suffers from” or “victim of” carry the assumption that a person with a disability has a reduced quality of life. Use neutral language when describing a person who has a disability, simply stating the facts.

...

### 7. Describing people without disabilities.
“Non-disabled” refers to someone who does not have a disability. According to the [University of Kansas Research & Training Center on Independent Living](http://rtcil.org/products/media/guidelines) , non-disabled is the preferred term when comparing people with and without disabilities.

## Transcription

So, also as a psychologist, have you seen an increase in anxiety, anxiety-related disorders over the course of the last few years with COVID with the way our kids had to deal with that, with things we’re seeing in the news, media, school shootings, all these things.

...

So right now, we know that anxiety disorders, depression, trauma symptoms have overall increased for children.

...

**The mental health team at CHOC curated the following resources on mental health topics common to kids and teens, such as depression, anxiety, suicide prevention and more.**
[View the mental health guides](https://choc.org/mental-health/)

must_do.rule: Include scenes where the character's anxiety is triggered by relatable, everyday experiences to normalize the condition for the audience.
Portray the character's hypervigilance as a functional early-warning system, reflecting a natural variation in brain differences rather than a defect.
Write action lines using neutral, objective language that simply states the facts of the character's anxiety without emotional overlay.
Include moments where the character actively takes charge of their fears rather than remaining entirely passive.

must_not_do.rule: Do not write a resolution where the character's anxiety is permanently cured or resolved by a single brave act.
Do not write comedic beats that play the character's anxiety symptoms for laughs or reduce them to a quirky personality trait.
Do not write action lines or dialogue that imply pity or assume the character has a reduced quality of life due to their anxiety.
Do not use coded language, negativistic terms, or pictorial metaphors in dialogue or action lines to describe the character's anxiety.
